t: Number of Good Ways to Split a String — Editorial
o: We must count split points i (1 <= i < n) where the number of distinct characters in s[0..i-1] equals the number of distinct characters in s[i..n-1]. A brute force that recomputes distinct counts for every split is O(n^2), too slow for n up to 1e5. The key observation is that as we move the split point one character to the right, only one character leaves the right side and joins the left side, so both distinct counts can be maintained incrementally. This suggests a single pass with two frequency arrays, or precomputing prefix/suffix distinct counts.
k: Moving the split point by one changes exactly one character's side, so both distinct counts update in O(1).
A character is 'present' on a side iff its frequency there is > 0; track counts of characters with nonzero frequency instead of sets for speed.
Precomputing suffix distinct counts lets you answer each split with an O(1) lookup after computing prefix counts in one pass.

a.i: Compute the number of distinct characters in every suffix s[i..n-1] once, scanning from the right. Then scan from the left maintaining a set of seen characters; at each split point i, compare the size of the left set with the precomputed suffix distinct count at i. Each comparison is O(1), giving O(n) total with O(n) extra space.
s: Scan i from n-1 down to 0, building suf[i] = number of distinct chars in s[i..n-1] using a boolean presence array.
Scan i from 0 to n-2, adding s[i] to a left presence array and tracking leftDistinct.
At each i (split after index i), if leftDistinct == suf[i+1], increment the answer.
a.t: O(n) — two linear passes over the string with O(1) work per character.
a.sp: O(n) — the suffix distinct-count array dominates; O(1) otherwise since the alphabet is fixed at 26.

a.n: Approach 2: Single Pass with Two Frequency Arrays (Optimal Space)
a.i: Start with all characters on the right and nothing on the left. Move each character from right to left one at a time; maintain freqLeft and freqRight arrays plus counters of how many characters have nonzero frequency on each side. When the two counters are equal after moving character i, split point i yields a good split. This avoids the O(n) suffix array entirely.
s: Fill freqRight with counts of all characters; rightDistinct = number of distinct chars in s; leftDistinct = 0.
For each i from 0 to n-2: decrement freqRight[s[i]] (if it hits 0, rightDistinct--), increment freqLeft[s[i]] (if it becomes 1, leftDistinct++).
If leftDistinct == rightDistinct, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n) — one pass to fill right frequencies and one pass over split points, O(1) per step.
a.sp: O(1) — only two fixed-size arrays of length 26 plus counters.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 2: it is optimal in both time and space and shows you can maintain incremental state across a sliding boundary. Approach 1 is a fine alternative if you find it easier to reason about precomputed suffix data. Pitfalls: remember both parts must be non-empty, so loop split points only from 1 to n-1 (or indices 0 to n-2 when splitting after index i); be careful to check equality *after* updating both sides for the current character; strings of length 1 have zero good splits. Edge cases worth testing: single character, all identical characters (answer n-1), and strictly increasing letters like "abcd" (answer 1). A likely follow-up: generalize to counting splits into k parts with equal distinct counts, or handle larger alphabets using hash maps.
